paragraphs.text: THE CONFERENCE OF THE FIRST DAY.

By order of the emperor, the Catholic bishops and the bishops of the party of Donatus held a conference and debated with one another. The proceedings took place before the tribune and notary Marcellinus, who acted as judge. The written record of those proceedings became very long, although the whole business could have been handled far more briefly. Those who knew that their case was not a good one first did all they could to stop the conference from taking place at all, and to keep the case itself from being argued. When they could not achieve this, they used the sheer bulk of the proceedings to make the record of what was done hard to read. It therefore seemed best to gather everything into this summary. Numbers are marked both in this short summary and in the record itself, so that anyone can easily find whatever he is looking for.
When both parties had entered, the first item read was the emperor's rescript. In it he ordered a conference to be held between these bishops, so that clear reasoning might refute superstition.

Second was read the judge's own edict, which he had sent throughout the province. It ordered that the bishops of both parties be summoned and gather at Carthage by the Kalends of June in order to confer. In that edict, without any order from the emperor, he gave back their basilicas to those Donatists who promised to come, so that he might draw them to the conference with favors as well. In the same edict he also offered to let them choose any other judge they wished to sit with him. He swore that he would decide as the truth persuaded him. The same edict also contains other things meant to encourage them to assemble.

Third was read another edict of the judge, which he posted when the bishops of both parties were already present in Carthage. It set out where and how the conference would be held, and it again mentioned and fixed the day named above. He directed each party to write back to him and say whether they accepted the provisions of the edict.

Fourth, the bishops of the party of Donatus demanded that their opponents state why they had been assembled. The judge put this off, so that everything done before the day of the conference could first be read in order. Then the notice of the Donatists was read. In it they said they did not accept what he had laid down in his edict, namely that only those bishops should come to the place of conference whom the rest had chosen to conduct the case. These would number thirty-six in all, eighteen from each side: seven from each side to debate with each other, seven more from each to be called in for counsel if needed, and four more from each to oversee the keeping and writing of the record. Instead they asked that all who had come should be present, so that their numbers might be seen, for they said their opponents had falsely claimed they were few. In the notice they said that they had all come, even the very oldest men, and that the only ones missing were those kept away by bodily illness. The notice contains other things as well.

Fifth was read the letter that the Catholics wrote back to the judge, as his edict had directed. In it they stated that they agreed to everything laid down in that edict. In the same letter they also bound themselves by a promise. If the truth of the church were shown to them to be in the party of Donatus, they would not seek the honor of bishops there, but would follow the Donatists' counsel for the sake of Christian salvation. If instead the truth of the church were shown to be in their own communion, they would not deny the Donatist bishops their episcopal honors. They would do this for the good of peace, so that those who received this favor might understand that what the Catholics detested in them was not Christian consecration but human error. If the congregations could not bear to have two bishops in one church, both bishops would step aside. Single bishops would then be appointed, to be ordained by those bishops who were found to be sole bishops in their own congregations. The same letter also mentioned the case of the Maximianists. The party of Donatus had condemned them, yet for the sake of its own peace it received some of them back with their honors intact, and it did not annul the baptism they had given in a sacrilegious schism. The letter contains other things as well.

Sixth was read another edict of the judge, which he had posted together with the Donatists' notice and the Catholics' letter mentioned above, to let the people know what each party had written back to him.

Seventh was read the letter the Catholics gave the judge in reply to the Donatists' notice. In it they granted what the Donatists had asked, that all who had come should be present in the place where the conference was to be held. From the Catholic bishops, however, only those whom the judge had specified in his edict would be present. In this way, if any disturbance broke out, as the Catholics greatly feared, the blame would not fall on those present in very small numbers, but rather on those who had wanted their whole crowd to be there. The same letter also set out the entire case. It aimed to show that the Catholic Church is not the party of Donatus. Rather, it is the church that bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world, beginning from Jerusalem, as sacred scripture says. Whatever wicked people were in it, who are to be separated by the judgment of God at the end, could do it no harm. Moreover, the Donatists' predecessors had been unable to prove anything even against Caecilian himself. He had been found and declared innocent by church courts, and above all by the court of the emperor, before whom they had accused him. The Donatists often stir up resentment over the emperors' orders issued on behalf of the Catholic Church, so the letter also recalled from holy scripture that kings decreed very severe penalties in their kingdoms against those who blasphemed God. It also recalled the case of the Maximianists. The Donatists had themselves pursued them in the public courts. Yet after condemning them, they received some of them back with their honors intact, and they did not destroy the baptism these men had given in schism. They even said that those to whom they had granted a period of grace, although they were in communion with Maximian, had not been polluted by contact with him. The letter contains other things as well. All these things were set out there in case the Donatists, on thinking it over and seeing how bad a case the party of Donatus had, should be unwilling to have all who had come enter the place of conference to the end that peace and unity might be achieved.

Eighth, the judge asked whether the party of Donatus, like the Catholics as he could see, had already chosen the men who would conduct the case it had taken up. The party of Donatus replied that the Catholics had already argued the case before it had even been settled who would argue it, because of the Catholic letter that summarized the whole case. Then they began to insist that the questions of the time limit, the mandate, the persons and the case should be dealt with first, and only after that should the merits of the matter be taken up. The judge ruled that the case had not been prejudiced in any way. He asked again whether his edict on fixing the number of disputants had been obeyed, since everything that had to be done ought to be done through these men. The Donatists then began to argue about the time limit, claiming that the case itself could not be heard because the deadline had passed. Four months from the date of the edict the judge had sent to the province had run out on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, as the court staff answered when asked. The emperor had ordered the case to be heard within four months, so they said the deadline had already passed. They asked for judgment to be given against the Catholics as if they had failed to appear, as though the Catholics had been absent, or the Donatists had ever come in to argue the case while the Catholics were away, or the Catholics had stayed away after being warned or summoned. They said these things by way of slander and evasion, and such arguments would not succeed lawfully even in a secular court. They simply did not want anything to be done. The judge himself answered them that both parties had agreed on the Kalends of June. Besides, even if one of the parties had still not appeared, there could have been two more months left, which the emperor had added and which had to be observed with three successive edicts.

Ninth: the judge had said earlier that using the time limit to keep the case from being heard was an objection for the law courts rather than for bishops. The party of Donatus took this as an opening to say that nothing should be done with them according to public law, but only according to the divine scriptures. When the judge asked what each party thought about this, the Catholics replied that he should order the mandate of the Catholic council to be read. That mandate laid down for the chosen disputants how they were to proceed, and from it, they said, it could more clearly be seen that they were proceeding not by courtroom evasions but by the testimony of God. The dispute dragged on for some time, with the Catholics pressing for the mandate to be read and the Donatists refusing. In the end the judge set aside all these delaying disputes and ordered the mandate to be read.

Tenth was read the mandate of the Catholic council. It charged the bishops chosen to debate with defending the Catholic Church against the accusations of the Donatists. In this mandate, as in the earlier letter, the whole case was again set out briefly. First, the case of the church, which is spread throughout the whole world as was promised, was to be kept separate from the case of Caecilian, whatever that case had been. This was meant to show that the wicked in the church cannot harm the good as long as the good do not consent to their evil deeds. Such wicked people are either unknown to the good or are tolerated by them for the sake of the unity of peace. The point was to be shown from the comparisons in the gospel, from the example of the prophets, of the Lord Christ himself, of the apostles and of bishops, and from the judgment of the Donatists themselves in the matter of the Maximianists. Next, it was to be shown by reliable documents that Caecilian's own case had not been a bad one. These documents would prove that both he and his consecrator, Felix of Abthugni, had been cleared, even though the Donatists had accused Felix with special venom in their council. The mandate also contains other things, concerning baptism and the persecution that the party of Donatus usually charges against the Catholics. For the case of the Maximianists was mentioned there again, as in the earlier letter. It showed that by their own judgment the Donatists had washed away every charge they usually bring against the Catholics, whether about baptism, persecution or being defiled by communion with others. It was also added that the Donatists might, even now, want to bring charges against Catholic bishops in order to cause delays. If so, the hearing and examination of these charges should be put off until later, so that the case that pressed first could be finished. The Catholics set out the whole case both in the earlier letter and in this mandate for the following reason. Rumor had it that the Donatists would try to bring in delaying pleas. If they were not allowed to do so, they might break off from the conference. In that event the case of the Catholic Church, though it had not been argued, would still remain in brief in the written record for people to read. Then it would be understood that the Donatists had feared that case and had therefore refused to confer.

Eleventh, the judge ruled that the Catholics' mandate put forward the testimony of God rather than legal snares, and ordered the signatures of all to be read. A dispute broke out and dragged on for some time. The Donatists demanded that those who had signed the mandate be present in person. They objected that the Catholics could have deceived the judge, in whose presence the men were recorded as having signed, by putting forward men who were not bishops. They also objected that the Catholics had added other bishops to ancient sees to swell their numbers. The Catholics resisted having their men brought in. They feared that the Donatists were preparing some disturbance that would break off the conference altogether, since the Donatists seemed entirely unwilling for it to take place. This was clearest when they tried to plead the time limit, as if the case had already lapsed and could not be heard. People thought the Donatists had not yet caused such a disturbance only because they saw that, if it happened, the blame could not fall on the Catholics, who were present in very small numbers, but would rather fall on themselves, since their whole crowd was there. But the Catholics gave way to their wish, and all who had signed came in. It then became clear that the Donatists had wanted this because they believed that not as many Catholics had come to Carthage as the signatures showed. It was thought they believed this because the Catholics had not entered Carthage with the same pomp as they had, and so the Donatists suspected that only a few had come.

Twelfth, the Catholic bishops whose presence had been demanded came in. All of them were read out one by one, and each stepped forward into the middle and was recognized by the Donatists, either by his neighbors or by those who shared the same town with him. Some Catholic bishops who were read out came from places where the party of Donatus had no presence. In those cases the Donatists themselves knew well enough that they had no colleagues or communion of their own there. They knew that there were Catholics there, either men they knew or men they had heard of in their own neighborhood. So it turned out that not a single Catholic's signature was read out whose presence they doubted. When they came to the name of Victorian, the Catholic bishop of Mustis, he stepped forward and answered that he had two rivals: Felician in the city of Mustis and Donatus at Turris. The Catholics demanded that it be put on record that Felician was in communion with Primian. The Donatists had condemned Felician among others along with Maximian, as one who had condemned Primian and ordained Maximian himself. Later they had received him back with his honor intact, and had not destroyed the baptism of those he had baptized in the schism of Maximian. But they refused to answer the Catholics' question, saying that this should not be demanded of them. When it was pressed more insistently, they said that this belonged to the main hearing of the case. The judge ruled in their favor: what had been begun should be carried on, and the other question could be looked into later if necessary. In that same diocese of Mustis it became plain that they themselves had added another bishop to an ancient see, the very thing they had charged against the Catholics out of empty spite. It was later shown that they had done the same in other places too.

Thirteenth: once the Catholics present who had signed had been reviewed and recognized, the judge offered [?] to let them conduct the proceedings seated rather than standing. The Donatists declined. They thanked him for offering seats to such old men, and in declining they said many things in praise of themselves and of the judge himself, which anyone who wishes may read in the record. This matters, because they praised him so highly as to call him honorable, just, reverent and kind, and yet they did not want the case to be heard before him, though so many had gathered to hear it.

Fourteenth, the Donatists' mandate was also produced and read. It was briefly worded: the men they had chosen were to act as if against their betrayers and persecutors. The names of the signers were also read out, because the Catholics had asked for this in order to establish whether they had signed in person at Carthage. But the Donatists pressed the judge much more insistently for this to be done, so that their own numbers might be seen, and they made it clear that they wanted this very much. In that reading some were found for whom others had signed in their absence. One man was also found who did not answer when his name was read, and the Donatists said he had died on the journey. The Catholics asked how a man who had died on the journey could have signed at Carthage. For a long time the Donatists wavered, confused and not knowing what to answer. First they said that what had been reported was not about him but about someone else. The Catholics took them to mean someone else, that is, a cleric who might have signed for the dead man, and so they asked whether the cleric had signed in his own name or in the dead man's name. But then the Donatists answered that the man had indeed signed in person when the mandate was drawn up on the eighth day before the Kalends of June. He had been ill when he signed, they said, and had died on the way back home. On hearing this the Catholics asked for the Donatists' earlier words to be read, so that the inconsistency, once caught, might be made clear. When this was done and the inconsistency was plain, the judge asked whether they would at least affirm, with God as their witness, that the man had been at Carthage when they all gathered in person to give the mandate and sign it. At this they became even more flustered and replied, “What if someone else presented himself in his place?” The judge left this falsehood, now exposed, to God's judgment and ordered the rest of the names to be read. When they had been read, he asked about the number of bishops on each side. The court staff replied that the Donatist bishops' names came to two hundred and seventy-nine. This total included those for whom others had signed in their absence, and it counted the dead man as well. It was established that the names of all the Catholics present came to two hundred and eighty-six. Twenty of these had not signed. Even so, they showed that they were present by stepping forward into the middle, and they declared for the record that they gave their mandate and consent. The only exceptions were those kept there in Carthage by illness. The place of conference was the Baths of Gargilius, since that place was later agreed upon. Of the Catholics who had signed the mandate, and of those who gave their mandate in person for the record, the only ones absent were those kept there in Carthage by ill health. But of those whose names appeared among the Donatist signatures, two groups were missing. One was made up of those the Donatists said were sick in Carthage. The other was made up of those for whom others had signed in their absence, that is, men who were not in Carthage at all. The Donatists kept boasting of their numbers, but it was already established that more Catholics had come to Carthage. Beyond this, the Catholics stated that another hundred and twenty of their bishops had not come to Carthage, being kept away by old age, by illness or by various other needs. When the Donatists heard this, they answered that far more of their own had not come to Carthage, and that they had many sees without bishops. Yet in the notice they had given the judge they had said quite plainly that they had all come to Carthage. Not even the oldest men, they had said, had been deterred by age or hardship, and the only ones who had not come were those kept in their sees or on the road by ill health. As for the sees they said were vacant on their side, the Catholics answered that they themselves had sixty for which successor bishops had not yet been ordained. So these signatures of the two parties showed two things: falsehoods were caught on the Donatist side, and their number of bishops was smaller. By their own account, only the sick had failed to come to Carthage, and yet others had signed for some of these who fell ill on the road. The signatures contained all their names, including those for whom others had signed, and these came to two hundred and seventy-nine. It is in no way believable that far more than a hundred and twenty of them, that is, a third of them all, could have been sick in their sees and for that reason failed to come to Carthage.

Fifteenth, all those whose presence was no longer needed went out, and only those whom each side had chosen as necessary remained. With the consent of both sides, the conference was then adjourned to the day after next, since the present day already seemed spent.
THE CONFERENCE OF THE SECOND DAY.

First, when they assembled at the place mentioned after an interval of one day, as had been agreed and arranged, the judge again offered them seats and asked that they sit. The Catholics sat down at once, but the Donatists refused. In refusing they said, among other things, that it was written that they should not sit with such people. The Catholics did not answer this at the time, so as not to cause delays, but did so at a more suitable point, in the conference of the third day. So the judge himself then replied that he would hear the case standing.

Second, the notice was read which they had submitted the day before. In it they asked that the Catholics' mandate be issued to them, so that after examining it they could appear prepared on the appointed day, since the stenographers could not manage to produce the written record in time. The judge's reply to this notice was also read, in which he ordered that what they asked should be done.

Third, the judge asked what they would answer about the signatures, that is, whether they accepted what he had laid down in his edict, that each party should sign its own statements. The Catholics answered that they had already expressed their consent to this in writing. The Donatists, however, said that they were greatly troubled by it, because it was not customary. When the judge asked whether they were satisfied with the number of persons appointed by each side to supervise the writing of the record, they began to ask for an adjournment, so that the written record could be issued to them and they could answer then. This started a long dispute with them, since the consent they had given to proceeding with the matter on that day was read out from the record again and again. When they said that they could not read the shorthand notes, and asked that the written-up record be issued to them first, the judge ordered the sealed codices that were being kept under guard to be brought, and what their own stenographers had taken down to be read out to them, so that they would not go back on their own consent. And when they kept making excuses about the issuing of the record, on the grounds that the stenographers had not managed to write it up, they were also told that they themselves had said in their notice that they had asked for the Catholics' mandate to be issued to them so that they could come prepared on the present day, precisely because the stenographers could not produce the record in time. Then, finding nothing to say, they tried once again to stir up the objection about the time limit, which had been answered more than sufficiently and had already been disposed of on the first day. But on this point too the Catholics then answered them: not only did the edict of the judge set the first of June as the date, but they themselves had drawn up their mandate on the twenty-fifth of May, when the day on which they claimed the case ought to have been heard, namely the nineteenth of May, had already passed. It was also stated that Primian himself had promised to appear by the first of June. The Catholics said all this because they had heard that the Donatists had been speaking about this matter among their own people in order to stir up ill will. Yet despite all this the Donatists persisted most vehemently in asking for an adjournment. When the Catholics saw that they were trifling at such length in order to load the record with a mass of words, they asked the judge to grant them the adjournment they sought. An adjournment of six days was granted, the stenographers having stated when the record could be ready, and the Donatists promising that once the record had been issued they would sign their own statements.
THE CONFERENCE OF THE THIRD DAY.

On the third day of the conference, that is, 8 June, after the parties had entered, the commissioner first asked whether the records had been released to them. The court staff replied that they had released them before the day they had promised, as the receipts of both parties would prove. The receipts were read out, and they established that the catholics had received the records on 6 June at the fifth hour of the day, and the Donatists on the same day at the third hour.

Second, when the commissioner had ordered that the main business should now be set out, the catholics said that they had long wanted to deal with the main business. This was that the Donatists should prove, if they could, the crimes they habitually allege against the church spread throughout the whole world. The Donatists replied that it should first be established who the parties bringing the action were, so that delays might be created by an examination of the persons. There was a long struggle over this. The catholics refused, and pressed hard for the superfluous evasions and delays to be set aside so that they might come to the case. The Donatists, on the other hand, insisted most stubbornly that the persons should be examined, and demanded that it be stated who had asked the emperor for this conference to be held. They wanted it established that the catholics were the plaintiffs, so that under the rules of the courts they could examine the persons of the plaintiffs. Yet the catholics' mandate had already been read out in the first session, and there they showed that they were not plaintiffs but defenders against the crimes that the Donatists habitually charge against their communion. Moreover, the Donatists themselves had earlier demanded that the church's case be argued not by courtroom formulas but rather by the testimonies of the divine scriptures. When the catholics' mandate was read, they had acknowledged that the catholics wished to support the church's case from the holy scriptures, and they had promised that they in turn would argue from the same authority of the divine law. Then, as if they had forgotten what they had demanded and what they themselves had promised, when the catholics proposed that the accusation and the vindication of the church should be dealt with, they began to ask for the persons of the plaintiffs, so that they could examine them under the rules of the courts. The catholics resisted this. To cut off the delays which they had heard the Donatists were preparing and which they could now see them weaving, they kept insisting that the church's case should be argued instead. In the course of the dispute it was agreed that the emperor's order commanding the conference to be held should be read, so that in this way the person of the plaintiff might be established. For the commissioner also thought that the persons of the plaintiffs should be determined first, so that the Donatists should not be refused anything, even under the rules of the courts, when they seemed to be asking for something just. So when the imperial order had been read, it was declared that the catholics had asked for the conference and that it had been granted. Then the Donatists began to demand also the petition by which the catholics had asked for the conference. When the commissioner himself answered them that a petition is not usually included in a pragmatic rescript, they turned instead to demanding that the catholics produce and disclose to them the mandate by which they had instructed that the conference be requested from the emperor, together with the envoys they had sent to obtain it. They claimed that they ought to examine what had been instructed, and that there they could find what [the catholics' instructions] had said about them to the emperor. The catholics understood that this was being asked in order to find pretexts for introducing long delays and postponements. They maintained that what the Donatists were asking for had nothing at all to do with the case, since the emperor himself showed most plainly that the conference had been requested by the catholics: he had appointed a commissioner so that clear reasoning might refute superstition. They urged strongly that all interposed delays and further inquiries should be set aside, and that the conference should instead do what the emperor had ordered it to do, since it was established that it had been requested from him and granted.

Meanwhile a few remarks and objections were also exchanged by both sides about the name "catholic" and which side had the better claim to it, and it was ordered that this be reserved for the main case. Some time later, when the name "catholic" was again mentioned and the Donatists said that the catholic church was rather on their side, the commissioner ruled that for the present, without prejudice to anyone, he could not call the catholics by any other name than the one used by the emperor who had appointed him commissioner. As for the Donatists, the more they claimed to be catholics, the more they ought now to set aside their interposed delays and argue the case itself, in which they could prove that they were the true catholics. The commissioner had made so many rulings against them, demanding that the case be argued instead and declaring that the persons of the envoys and the mandate given to them had nothing to do with the case, and that he had not been instructed to inquire into such things. Yet after all these delays and rulings, the Donatists said that if the catholics refused to obey the rulings by disclosing the envoys and the mandate given to them, they should at least answer whether they stood in the position of plaintiffs. The catholics were greatly surprised that the Donatists said they were not obeying the rulings in the matter of producing the envoys' mandate, when in fact the commissioner had given so many rulings against the Donatists themselves. So the catholics asked which rulings they had not obeyed. When the Donatists gave no answer to this, the commissioner ruled that the catholics should answer the Donatists' question about the position of plaintiff. They answered that their proposal was this: that the crimes the Donatists habitually charge against their communion should be either proved or refuted, so that the separation of the Donatists might be either defended or corrected. Then, when the commissioner demanded a reply from the Donatists, they answered that the Africans who called themselves catholics wanted to defend someone else's case, that is, the church of the whole world. Nothing, they said, ought to be prejudged against them concerning that church, since this matter was being debated among Africans; rather, they should wait for the church overseas, so that whichever side won would be seen to belong to it and would have the name "catholic." But at the end of their statement they again demanded an answer about the person of the plaintiff. Here the catholics answered both points briefly: the question about the persons had already been settled by the first and second rulings; and it was they, not the Donatists, who were in communion with the church spread throughout the whole world, to which the divine scripture bears witness, and so they were rightly catholics and rightly called catholics. The Donatists replied that the name "catholic" was derived not from the universality of the nations but from the fullness of the sacraments, and they asked the catholics to prove that all the nations were in communion with them. The catholics welcomed this most gladly and asked to be allowed to prove it. But the Donatists once again began to rake up the question of the mandate given to the envoys, which they had asked to be produced for them, and once again to recoil from the church's case, which had now come into the open for discussion. At one moment they demanded the mandate mentioned above; at another they pressed for the person of the plaintiff to be established; at another they demanded that the commissioner give a ruling on these very things they had asked for, although he had already ruled on them so many times and had declared that they were asking for them in vain.

The commissioner considered that they were not right to ask for the mandate given to the envoys to be produced for them, since what was sufficient for the case was established: the conference had been requested and granted. Nevertheless, he did not think it unjust of them to ask for the person of the plaintiff to be established. But the catholics had already been told beforehand, and could see well enough from the Donatists' purpose, that the only reason they were seeking the persons of the plaintiffs was to be able to introduce very long delays and postponements through an examination of the persons. They strongly wished not to come to the case, because they knew full well that they had nothing to say in it, as the event itself later revealed, though late. Seeing this, then, the catholics refused to take on the role of plaintiffs. They maintained that they were not bringing charges but defending against charges brought, and that once they had defended against them and shown them to be false, it would follow that it would become clear who the Donatists were and how wickedly they had separated themselves from unity. At this the Donatists maintained that if the catholics, in whatever way, of their own accord compelled their opponents to answer them, even about the very crimes they wished to refute, then they held the role of plaintiffs. But the catholics replied that they had asked for the conference not in order to bring charges to be refuted, but in order to refute the charges brought. For both the Donatists' mandate, drawn up against "traitors and persecutors," and the words of Primian when he was first approached by the catholics about a conference, testified that he was bringing a charge against them. He had said: "It is unworthy that the sons of the martyrs and the offspring of the traitors should meet together." And although he had then refused to confer, he had later said, in the court of the prefects, that he wished to be heard and to have the matter examined. Holding the Donatists to this agreement about a conference, the catholics had asked the emperor that it be held.

Then the commissioner ordered them to prove now the crimes they had charged, and ruled that the person of the plaintiff should not be determined from who had requested the conference, if both sides were shown to have requested it. At this the Donatists began once again to ask him to give a ruling about the person. The commissioner gave a ruling, saying that if both parties had requested the conference, the plaintiff was the one who brought the charges. Then the Donatists demanded that the catholics prove whether both sides had requested the conference. When the commissioner said, "The catholics will have to prove this," there arose once again a delaying dispute about the name "catholic" and the names "Donatists" and "Caecilianists." Next the catholics produced the records of the proceedings in the court of the prefecture, to prove that the Donatists too had requested the conference. When the commissioner ordered these to be read, the Donatists went back again to matters already dealt with and began to demand that the commissioner rule on the very things on which he had ruled so many times, namely the question of the person and the envoys' mandate, which they had so needlessly demanded be produced for them so many times. As far as could be understood, they were doing this because they feared that the prefecture's records would be read, in which they had damaged their own case with certain thoughtless and rash answers. So there was a long struggle on their part, chiefly with the commissioner himself. They asked that the mandate given to the envoys be produced for them, or that he rule that they had asked for it needlessly; he, for his part, said that he had already ruled, and ruled that this had nothing whatever to do with the present proceedings, since the imperial letter made clear what had been requested and what granted. At last, at his order, they began to read the prefecture's records. When the date and the consuls of these records had been read, the Donatists immediately interrupted again and began to demand those same matters already dealt with. But when the commissioner ruled that the records ought to be read so that the person of the plaintiff might be established, they began to argue on the contrary that there were earlier records, which ought to be read instead. The catholics replied that the Donatists did not want the prefecture's records read because they dreaded the statements they had made in them.

So the Donatists produced the records of the proconsul and of the vicar of the prefecture. In these the catholics had asked that the Donatists be summoned through municipal records, so that by a conference between the two sides the error might be removed from their midst; this was long before they had asked the emperor for this conference. By these records the Donatists wanted to show that the catholics stood in the position of plaintiffs, because there the catholics had said that the Donatists, as heretics, were committing many offences against divine and human laws. Against this the catholics said that even then they had demanded a conference so that they might answer the Donatists' charges on behalf of the church. So they repeatedly asked that, if records were to be read on the ground that they were established to be earlier, then rather those should be read in which the Donatists had first sent the case of Caecilian to the Emperor Constantine, accusing him through the proconsul Anullinus. The records the Donatists were producing were read, but those from the court of the prefects, which had already begun to be read, were not. Then a dispute began: if the records produced by the Donatists had been preferred to those produced by the catholics on the ground that they were found to be earlier, and were therefore read instead, then at least after they had been read, those far earlier records should also be read, which would show that in this whole case under discussion the Donatists had originally been the accusers, through the proconsul before the emperor. The Donatists fought hard to prevent these from being read, resisting with many and varied statements, just as they had fought and wrung out a decision that the prefecture's records should not be read. In the course of this struggle they kept repeating the worn-out demand, rejected by so many rulings of the commissioner, that the envoys' mandate be produced for them. They also repeated a question that had already been settled before, whether the catholics preferred to argue from the testimonies of the law or from public records. They said that if the catholics chose the testimonies of the divine law, they should give up all public laws and records; but if they preferred to argue from public laws and records, they should leave aside the divine proofs. And yet, if the catholics chose to argue rather from the evidence of public records, the Donatists said that they would not allow even this, namely that the records offered by the catholics be read, because they had a valid time-limit objection. This was, of course, the one to which both the catholics and the commissioner himself had given them a sufficient answer: they were saying that the case itself had lapsed and could no longer be argued, because the day had passed on which four months were completed. It was evident that they greatly feared the reading of records showing that Caecilian had originally been accused before the emperor by their predecessors, and had then been acquitted and cleared by both ecclesiastical and imperial judgments. In other words, they feared that the very case for which they had come would actually be argued, since they felt that there they could be defeated quite plainly. So unwilling and afraid were they that they were even forced to admit it, saying that they were being led into the case "sensim," that is, little by little, and drawn into the inner matters of the case. This is surely what they ought to have wished for, if they had trusted not in empty and delaying objections but in the truth of the case itself.

The catholics, then, were striving hard to come to the case, which they saw the Donatists had no wish at all to reach; yet again and again they answered the very points that the Donatists kept repeating, though these had already been settled so many times. Two matters had come into the open: one about producing the mandate given to the envoys, the other whether the catholics preferred to argue from the divine testimonies or from public records. On producing that mandate, the catholics answered that it had nothing at all to do with the Donatists or with the present case. And the commissioner himself ruled again what he had often ruled before: that he could not examine at all the person of the envoys or the mandate they had received, and that he ought not to depart from what had been entrusted to him, since it was clear enough from the imperial letter appointing him judge in this case that the emperor had granted the conference. On the other matter, where they asked which the catholics would choose, the divine proofs or the public records, the catholics replied many times as follows. If the Donatists did not charge men with crimes, as they were accustomed to charge them as traitors, but the only question was what and where the church was, then the catholics would make no use of public records but only of the testimonies of the divine scriptures. If, however, the Donatists persisted in that accusation and incrimination of men, then, since they themselves could not demonstrate such things except by such records, the catholics too would undoubtedly defend against crimes of this kind by public records; for otherwise such things could be neither charged nor defended. This was repeated and impressed on them many times by the catholics and by the commissioner himself, while they returned to the same points and repeated the same things in many and varied ways and in many statements, so that the case would not be argued and the records they saw already at hand would not be read. But at last the commissioner overcame such prolonged obstinacy and ordered the documents submitted by the catholics to be read, and the case for which so many bishops of both parties had assembled finally began to be argued. It turned out remarkably that, although the Donatists were seeking the person of the plaintiff in order to avoid coming to the case, this very inquiry into the plaintiff suddenly brought the case into the open.

Third, then, the following took place. The report of the proconsul Anullinus to the Emperor Constantine was read. When the Donatists asked where it had been brought from, the catholics answered that if they had doubts, it could be looked for in the proconsul's archive. This report states most plainly that the Donatists themselves had originally sent an accusation to the Emperor Constantine, through the proconsul just mentioned, setting out the crimes they were charging against Caecilian. When it had been read through, the Donatists began to ask whom the catholics called their father. The catholics answered them in accordance with the gospel, where it is written: "Call no one on earth your father; for you have one Father, God." Yet even after hearing this, the Donatists nonetheless began to ask whether Caecilian was their father or their mother. The catholics had already said that he was neither their father nor their mother but their brother: a good brother if he was good, a bad one if he was bad, since even a bad man would be a brother because of the sacraments they shared. Even so, there was a fairly long dispute over this, the Donatists repeating the same questions and the catholics giving the same answers. For the Donatists also raised the objection of how the apostle could say: "For though you have many tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel." The catholics answered that this was said as a mark of honour, on account of the mystery of the gospel which the apostle was administering; for with regard to faith and eternal salvation there is no father but God. The apostle could not have said anything contrary to Christ. When Christ said, "Call no one on earth your father; for you have one Father, God," the apostle would not, as though resisting Christ's words, call himself the father of those to whom he had preached the gospel, unless a distinction were certainly to be drawn between what is said with regard to divine grace and what is said as a mark of human honour.

They also asked who had ordained Augustine, preparing some slanders or other, as was being rumoured. He answered them without fear that he had been ordained by Megalius, who was then the primate of the bishops of the catholic church in Numidia, and he pressed them urgently to bring out now what they had prepared, so that there too they might be shown to be slanderers. But they turned their attack to something else, going back to the person of Caecilian. The catholics said that he did no harm to the church even if real crimes of his were shown, and yet that no real crimes of his could be shown.

Then the Donatists produced a letter which they said they had received from their whole council. It was meant to answer the Catholics' mandate, which had been entered on the first day of the proceedings. On the following day, before the second session was held on the third, the Donatists had submitted a formal notice asking for this mandate to be issued to them, so that they could come to the hearing prepared. Perhaps it was in order to write this letter carefully that they also asked for an adjournment at the second session, and they were granted one of six days. So in the fourth place the following was done. The Donatists' letter, mentioned above, was read out; in it they had tried to answer the Catholics' mandate, which is included in the record of the first session. Anyone willing to read and weigh both documents will find that they were unable to answer that mandate. First, the mandate had drawn testimonies from the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the apostolic and gospel writings, showing that the Catholic Church spreads through the whole world, beginning from Jerusalem. From there, growing into places near and far, it came to Africa too. It also spread into the other places and cities through which it was first extended, where many churches belonging to the one Church were founded by the labour of the apostles, and it is plain that the Donatists are not in communion with these churches. The Donatists were unwilling not only to discuss these testimonies but even to touch on them at all. Nor in so long a letter did they dare to bring forward a single testimony from the holy scriptures to claim that the church of Donatus' party had been foretold and announced in advance, as the Catholics had brought forward so many on behalf of the Church with which they are in communion, which begins from Jerusalem and spreads through the whole world. So they left this part of those many testimonies entirely untouched and passed over it, as if it had not been said in the Catholic mandate they claimed to be answering. Instead they tried to show, citing many testimonies of the divine scriptures, that the Church of God was not foretold as one that would include a mixture of wicked people. Yet afterwards they came to the gospel parable that the Catholics had included in their mandate, about the nets cast into the sea, in which the Lord said that every kind of fish is gathered and that the good are separated from the bad on the shore, that is, at the end of the age. Here they themselves admitted that hidden wicked people, at least, are mixed into the Church. But they said that the weeds were mixed with the wheat not in the Church but in the world itself, because the Lord says: "The field is this world." As for the threshing floor, where the Catholics had said the chaff remains mixed in until the time of winnowing, they did not even try to explain this parable, as though nothing of the kind were written in the gospel at all. Instead, as if the Catholics had made it up themselves, they merely found fault with it on the basis of a testimony from the prophet Jeremiah, who says: "What has chaff to do with wheat?" They did not notice what he was speaking about when he said this. He was not speaking about the Church, but about the divine visions of the prophets and human dreams, so that the two should in no way be compared. The parable of the sheep and the goats, which graze together and will be separated at the end of the age, which the Catholics had cited from the gospel among others, they refused to touch at all. For there they could not say that the shepherds do not see the goats in the common pastures, as they had said that the fishermen cannot see the bad fish in the sea among the nets.

Again, the Catholics in their mandate had wanted to show that the wicked are tolerated by the good in the Church and that the good are not polluted by contact with the wicked. To this end they cited the examples of the prophets, of the Lord Christ himself, and of the apostles, and after these the examples of good bishops, and also the judgment of the Donatists themselves, who denied that certain of their own members who had been in the schism of Maximian were polluted by contact with Maximian. In their letter the Donatists tried to answer these points and said what they could about the prophets, the Lord Christ and the apostles, but about the bishops and the Maximianists they kept silent. In the matter of the bishops they were pressed hard by the authority of Cyprian. The Catholics had quoted his words from one of his letters in their mandate, and these showed very plainly two things: that he taught that the wicked should be tolerated in the Church for the sake of unity, and that the Church should not be abandoned on their account; and that he himself tolerated within the Church certain of his colleagues, though he utterly abhorred their wicked ways and did not keep silent about their very evil deeds. Weighed down by his authority, the Donatists said something about the prophets, the Lord Christ and the apostles, in support of their claim that the wicked mixed into the Church are not to be tolerated, but they would say nothing whatever about the bishops. And yet Cyprian himself understood and wrote about Judas the traitor, and about those whom Paul tolerated when they proclaimed Christ out of envy, just as the Catholics set it out in their mandate: that the Lord bore with Judas as an example of tolerating the wicked in the Church, and that Paul bore with the people he spoke of in this way not outside the Church but within it. As for the Maximianists, what could they answer, when the men were still alive by whom they could be convicted most openly and most easily? The Catholics had said in their mandate that these same Maximianists had been driven out of their basilicas by the Donatists through public lawsuits. To this the Donatists somehow tried to answer that they had not brought criminal charges or forced anyone into their communion against his will, but had reclaimed their own property, or that of their people, by civil action. They forgot what Primian had once instructed to be stated on the record: "They take away what belongs to others; we let go of what has been taken from us." But the mandate also said of the Maximianists that the Donatists had received men they had themselves condemned with their rank undiminished, that they had denied that Maximian's associates were polluted by him, and that they had chosen to approve the baptism given by them in schism rather than annul and repeat it. To these points they did not attempt even a slight answer. They passed over them all in a remarkable silence, as if they had never been said.

Then there was baptism itself. In that mandate the Catholics had said that the apostle spoke of certain people who "hold the truth in iniquity," to show that it is possible for a truth that must not be destroyed to be held in an iniquity that must be destroyed. The Donatists either did not understand this, or chose to obscure with their words what they had understood, so that others would not understand it. They said that the apostle was speaking about the error of the Gentiles, as if it mattered whose error he was speaking of, when he showed all the same that truth can be held in iniquity. So when these two are found in one person, the truth is approved and the iniquity is corrected. This is what the Catholic Church does when it recognizes and embraces the truth of the sacrament in the Donatists, but detests and corrects the heretical iniquity in them. The Catholics had also said in the mandate that the baptism of Christ is not to be destroyed because heretics too administer it, just as Christ is not to be denied because demons too confess him. Here likewise the Donatists either did not understand or wished to obscure the point. They said that the Catholics had spoken against the martyrs, without saying which martyrs they meant, and they also said that the Catholics wanted to be in communion with demons. [?] [The answer was that there is no] communion with heretics when their iniquity is anathematized, even though the baptism found in their rite of consecration is not destroyed, just as the iniquity of the demons is anathematized even though the name of the Lord heard in their confession is not denied.

They also wrote a great deal in their letter about the persecutions they complain of suffering. Yet they did not dare to answer the point made in the Catholics' mandate, that they themselves were the first to accuse Caecilian before the Emperor Constantine, though they now complain about the emperors' laws. To stir up hatred against the Catholics they exaggerated both the deaths that their circumcellions inflict on themselves and everything they suffer under the public laws and penalties, not for being in the communion of Donatus but for the crimes with which they rage violently and live wickedly. They even dared to bring up the town of Bagai, where it has been made plain how many evils they committed and how much less they suffered.

The Catholics' mandate had also spoken of the clearing and acquittal of Caecilian and of Felix of Abthugni, whose alleged crimes the Donatists habitually used to stir up great hatred against the Catholics among the uninformed. Though the whole case they had come for turned on this point, they chose to give no answer to it at all in so long a letter. In what they said, and tried to support with divine testimonies, namely that the wicked are not to be tolerated in the Church but that one must withdraw from them because of the contagion of their sins, they showed that they meant it in such a way as to admit that no one can be stained by the sins of others when those sins are unknown. For they had said this about the bad fish as well: just as fishermen do not see the bad fish hidden in the waves, even though they are already inside the nets, so priests do not know the wicked hidden in the Church and are therefore in no way polluted by them. Yet in a letter so long, written with so long an adjournment granted, they did not try, even slightly or feebly, to prove the thing the Catholic mandate laid most stress on. They needed to prove not only that Caecilian's crimes were real, for that is not enough, but also that those crimes could have been proved to the Church that is spreading through all nations to the ends of the earth, and become known to it, so that, at least on their own terms, the Church could then have been stained by contagion with sins it knew about.

When the Donatists' letter had been read out, the judge wanted the document the Catholics had submitted for reading to be read as well. But the Donatists began to demand an answer to what they had written. The Catholics preferred this too, so that the letter would not stand as though it could not be answered. But when the Catholics began to reply, the Donatists began to interrupt and make a din, so that the reply could not run on uninterrupted, as their own letter had been read out with no one interrupting. The Catholics wanted to show how the divine testimonies that they themselves had cited, and those the Donatists had cited, should be understood, so that they would not be found to contradict each other, since both were divine and must surely agree rather than disagree. They began by speaking of the parable of the threshing floor. At this the Donatists interrupted and said that nothing about a threshing floor is found written in the gospel. When the Catholics cited the passage of the gospel more precisely, they interrupted again and said that the chaff to be winnowed later meant hidden wicked people. From there, amid their din and interruptions, a dispute arose about the weeds and the wheat over the word "world." Because it is written, "The field is this world," the Donatists would not have "world" understood as the Church. They cited many testimonies in which holy scripture used the word "world" only of the wicked, such as: "If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him," and others like it, as if this showed that the Church could not possibly be meant by the word "world." The Catholics, on the other hand, cited other testimonies showing that the word "world" is used in a good sense, such as: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself," and others of this kind, where the Church is meant, since it is the Church that is reconciled to God through Christ. All this went on while the Catholics tried to keep their speech going without a break and the Donatists made a din to prevent it. The Donatists did not hold back their reply, as the Catholics had done while their letter was being read, but kept interjecting objections to stop the Catholics' argument from proceeding undisturbed.

So the Catholics asked them to be patient, and only just obtained it after the judge had intervened many times. Then they answered the Donatists' letter. They showed by many testimonies and examples from the holy scriptures that the wicked are now so mixed into the Church that, although church discipline must stay watchful in rebuking them, not only with words but also with excommunication and deposition, nevertheless those who lie hidden in it are not known, and often even those who are known are tolerated for the sake of the peace of unity. In this way they showed that the divine testimonies agree. The testimonies that present the Church as mixed with the wicked describe its present time, as it is in this age. The testimonies that present it as having no wicked mixed in describe the time to come, as it will be in the age to come for ever. Now it is mortal, that is, it consists of mortal human beings, but then it will be immortal, when no one in it will die. In the same way Christ himself was mortal for its sake in this time, but after the resurrection he dies no more, and death will no longer have dominion over him; and this he will also grant to his Church at the end of the age. They said that these two times of the Church, what it is now and what it will be then, were also signified by two catches of fish. The first came before Christ's resurrection, when he ordered the nets to be cast without naming either the left side or the right, to teach that within the nets of his sacraments there would be neither the wicked alone nor the good alone, but the wicked mixed with the good. The second came after the resurrection, when he ordered the nets to be cast on the right side, so that we should understand that after our resurrection only the good will be in the Church. There will be no more heresies and schisms there, by which the nets are now torn. For the gospel did not fail to record that at the first catch the nets were torn, while of the last catch it says: "And although the fish were so large, the nets were not torn." It is of such a Church, they said, that it is said that the uncircumcised and unclean will not pass through it. For schismatic separations belong to the unclean, and then there will be none, because the nets were not torn. This was also signified, they said, when the raven, an unclean bird, went out of the ark and did not return. Yet when the raven went out, the ark was certainly not rid of all unclean animals. Clean and unclean were in it until the flood, as good and wicked are in the Church until the end of the age. But just as Noah offered sacrifice not from the unclean animals but from the clean, so it is not the wicked in the Church but the good who come to God.

The Donatists had said in their letter that the prophets were not in communion with those against whom they spoke such harsh words. About the prophets the Catholics answered that there was one temple which everyone used, and that none of the prophets who said such things against the wicked set up another temple, other sacrifices or other priests for himself. The Donatists had also cited testimonies of scripture in their letter to show that the sins of parents extend to their children too, though this has never rightly been understood except of children who imitate their parents' iniquities. To this the Catholics answered as follows. The divine oracles said such harsh and bitter things against that people, things the Donatists themselves cited in their letter, that it might seem no good person was left there. Yet not only were those same holy prophets there, but there also arose from that very people those whom the Lord himself found praiseworthy at his coming in the flesh, such as Zechariah and Elizabeth, John their son, the aged Simeon and Anna the widow. From this it is clear how impiously and slanderously the crimes of Caecilian were charged against the Catholics spread through the whole world. Simeon, Anna and others like them could not be charged with the crimes of the people into which they had been born and in whose sacraments they had been consecrated, though those crimes had been charged against that people not by human opinion but by the word of God. They also cited the prophetic testimony in which those who groaned over the crimes being committed in their midst were marked with a sign so that they would not perish with the wicked, and yet they were not separated from them in body.

Next they set out what kind of separation from the ungodly and the wicked the good must make in this time, so as not to share in the sins of others: a separation, namely, of heart, and of a different life and way of behaving. They said that the scripture, "Come out from among them, depart from there, and touch nothing unclean," must be understood in no other way than this: set yourselves apart by living differently, and do not consent to uncleanness. At this point too, very fittingly, the Donatists were answered on what they had said when the judge asked them to sit down: that it was written for them not to sit with such people. For when the Catholics were answering their letter, they said that separation from the wicked in this time is not to be understood as the Donatists had understood it when they refused to sit with them as though with the ungodly, because it is written: "I have not sat in the council of the ungodly." Surely, if they thought the Catholics ungodly, they ought not to have kept silent about what is forbidden next in the same psalm, where it goes on: "Nor will I go in with those who do evil." Since, then, they had gone in with those they thought ungodly, why did they not sit down with them too, so that in both cases they would be seen to have avoided a spiritual, not a bodily, sitting and entering together? Here too the case of the Maximianists was raised, which had already been put to them so many times. In it they said that neither they themselves nor those to whom they had granted a period of grace, men who had been in Maximian's schism and were his associates in condemning Primian, were polluted by contact with him. Yet these are the same people who maintained that the Christian world, to the ends of the earth, had perished through the crimes of Caecilian.

To this the Donatists could not answer the very powerful proofs from scripture or their own example in the matter of the Maximianists. So they went back to a point that had already been dealt with, saying that the "world" in which the wheat and the weeds were ordered to grow together cannot properly be understood as the Church. Yet the Catholics had already cited many divine testimonies showing that "world" is also used in a good sense, and that in this sense it can mean nothing but the Church. They had also shown that however "world" is taken, since both seeds grow throughout the world, the wheat of the whole world must not be abandoned because of the weeds. So although all this had already been said and the question itself seemed settled, they returned to it again out of sheer lack of anything to say, repeating the same points in the same terms. They asked how the devil could have sown weeds in the Church. Then they falsely charged the Catholics with speaking of two churches, one that now has the wicked mixed in, and another that would not have them after the resurrection. As if the saints who will reign with Christ will not be the very same people who now live justly for his name and bear with the wicked!

To this the Catholics replied that the Donatists themselves had already admitted that there were wicked people in the church, at least hidden ones. In turn they asked how the devil had sown these in the church, since the Donatists were raising this very question about the tares as though it could not happen. The Catholics also repeated the testimony of Cyprian, who understood this same Gospel parable in no other way than to say that there are tares in the church, and that they are not hidden but seen. The Donatists had not dared to make any reply at all to this testimony, although they hold Cyprian's authority in such high regard that they try to use it to defend their wrong views and practice of repeating baptism. The Catholics also refuted their misrepresentation about two churches, showing again, more explicitly, what they had said. They had not said that the church which now has the wicked mixed in it is something other than the kingdom of God, where the wicked will not be mixed in. They had said that the one and the same holy church is now in one condition and will later be in another: now it has the wicked mixed in, then it will not. In the same way it is now mortal, because it consists of mortal human beings, but will then be immortal, because no one in it will die, not even in body. In the same way, too, there are not two Christs just because he first died and afterward will not die. They also spoke of the outer and the inner man: these are different, yet they are not called two men. How much less should there be said to be two churches, when the very same people who now, being good, tolerate the wicked mixed among them and die so as to rise again will then neither have the wicked mixed among them nor die at all! There was also the matter of number. The Donatists had commended one church by the testimony of the scriptures, as though against the two churches which they boasted the Catholics had asserted. The Catholics replied that many churches are also spoken of in the scriptures, including the seven to which John writes, and yet these many are understood to be members of that single church. From this it would be clear that far less ought "two churches" to be held against them, since they had only said that the one and same church is not now such as it will be at the resurrection, when the apostolic writings are not reproached for speaking of the many churches of which the one church consists. To this the Donatists once more kept repeating the same things. Besides this, they added, playing on prejudice, that the Catholics had called the church mortal. They denied it was mortal because the Trinity, by whose grace the church is consecrated, is immortal, and because Christ died for it in order to make it immortal, as if the Catholics had said that it is not made immortal by the grace of God and by the Savior's blood shed for it. But the Catholics said that the times must be distinguished. There is the present, in which all the saints die, just as Christ himself died. And there is the future, in which they will rise and, with none of them ever to die, will live with him who has already risen.

While this was going on between them, and the Donatists in their contentiousness kept repeating superfluous points, however plain and clear the matters were, the commissioner promised to judge in his final sentence the matters he had heard enough about. He ordered them instead to take up the question of where the first cause of the division arose. Then the Donatists began to press him to judge first the matters he had heard. The Catholics also demanded this, but he held to what he had said and ordered them instead to take up this other matter, so that the cause of the first division might be shown. The Catholics then asked that the documents they were offering be read. When he had ordered this done, the Donatists began to resist more stubbornly and to press him to judge now the matters already examined. They repeated the same points that had already been dealt with. They added that he ought not to judge at all the case he wanted taken up by reading the documents the Catholics had offered. They said that Christ ought to be the judge of this case, stirred up resentment against the Catholics for having asked for a man as judge, and also said their usual things about the persecutions they were supposedly suffering. To this the Catholics replied that the Donatists ought not to stir up resentment over asking for a human judge. They themselves had judged the case of the Maximianists without reserving it for Christ as judge, and as accusers they had originally sent the very case of Caecilian to a man, that is, to the emperor Constantine. Nor should they stir up resentment over persecutions, on the grounds that the Catholics asked something of the emperors on the church's behalf, when their own circumcellions, led by clergy, were committing such horrible crimes. The Donatists' reply to this, that it had nothing to do with bishops, was in vain, since it was alleged that those men did such things under the leadership of clergy.

At that point it was also said that they had attacked people's eyes with lime and vinegar. In this crime they outdid the devil in cruelty, since he did not do this to the flesh of the holy man that he had received power to afflict. Here the Donatists asked whether it is those who do such things who are sons of the devil, or those who suffer them, as if the Catholics had been speaking of anything other than their own sufferings, the most savage kind, at the hands of the Donatist clergy and circumcellions. Yet here too the Catholics took the opportunity they were given and did not fail to throw the Maximianists in their faces. They said that by the Donatists' own reasoning the Maximianists were better, since the Donatists had persecuted them before three or more proconsuls: if the Maximianists suffered, it was the Donatists who inflicted it. The Catholics pressed them to answer whether they had not received back Felicianus, one of those whom they had condemned and persecuted, and whether they did not have him among their colleagues. To this objection they fell completely silent, as always, and turned to something else. They charged the Catholics with defending the devil, because the Catholics had said that he spared the eyes of holy Job, and that these men had therefore outdone him in cruelty. And they set about accusing the devil, as though the Catholics had defended him. They said that he had been more cruel in sparing the eyes in Job's flesh, so that they would remain to look at the wound he had inflicted on the whole body. It is very surprising that they wanted to make so much of this. Perhaps they meant it to be understood that those who attacked people's eyes had acted kindly, so that their victims would not be tormented by seeing the wounds they had received from them all over their bodies.

But the Donatists again exaggerated the persecutions they suffer and recalled certain deaths of their people in the town of Bagai. The Catholics replied that they had suffered this while their violence was being resisted, violence which they had even attempted to inflict on the judge. The Catholics recalled that the Donatists had committed horrible crimes in that town, so that even a basilica was burned and holy books were thrown into the fire. Their deaths, they said, came rather from their habit of throwing themselves off cliffs. The Donatists in reply kept exaggerating what they called the persecutions they suffered. They boasted that these fruits showed their adversaries to be a bad tree, and asked again and again for a ruling about the field, the tares, and the one immortal church. The Catholics, for their part, recounted the Donatists' fruits: schisms, rebaptisms, and the fact that their own forebears had been the first to bring accusations before the emperor. The conflict went on for a long while in mutual charges of this sort, until the commissioner chose to put a stop to all of it. He promised to give judgment on these matters in his later sentence, and ordered the reading of what the Catholics had offered, which had already begun to be read and had been interrupted. Thus the case of the church was concluded. The Catholics had taken great pains to keep it distinct from the case of Caecilian, since the church, having earned so many divine testimonies against all human accusations, could not be prejudged by anyone's crimes. From this point the case of Caecilian also began to be dealt with.

In the fifth place, then, the following was done. Two reports of the proconsul Anullinus to the emperor Constantine were read. One, which had already been read earlier, showed that the forebears of the Donatists, that is, the party of Majorinus, had given him documents with charges against Caecilian and asked that they be sent to Constantine, and that he had sent them to the emperor. The other showed that, by order of the same emperor, he had met with them so that each side would send ten men to plead the case, and that they had promised to do so. Then the letter of that same emperor to the bishops was also read, in which he charged them with hearing Caecilian's case. After that, in order, the reading began of the episcopal judgment given in the city of Rome by Miltiades, bishop of Rome, and the other bishops of Gaul and Italy who sat with him. The first part of this judgment, that is, the proceedings of the first day, was read. There the accusers of Caecilian who had been sent said that they had nothing to say against him. There, too, Donatus of Casae Nigrae was convicted in person of having made a schism at Carthage while Caecilian was still a deacon; for it was out of the schism at Carthage that the party of Donatus arose against the Catholic Church. There also these same opponents of Caecilian were charged with having withdrawn persons necessary to the case. They promised to produce them on another day, but this was a lie, and they refused to come to the judgment any more. When this part of the judgment had been read and the reading of what was done on another day had begun, the Donatists interrupted. They began demanding most insistently that what they were offering be read first, asserting that it was out of order to read first the acquittal of Caecilian, whom they had not yet accused. They argued about this for quite a while. The Catholics said that what had already begun to be read should not be interrupted until all the proceedings of that judgment were finished. The Donatists, on the contrary, asserted that what was being interrupted ought not even to have been started, since it was not proper for a man to be defended before he had been accused. To this the Catholics replied that, when the commissioner was asking about the cause of the schism, they had asked for the reading of documents which had been offered for reading when the question of who was the plaintiff was being dealt with. They had wanted them read for two reasons. The first was to make it plain that the Donatists, who were stirring up resentment against the Catholics because a man sat as commissioner in this conference, had been the first to ask for a human judge in this case. The second was to establish who the plaintiff was. And since the reading had begun, it ought not to be interrupted but carried through to the end. Meanwhile, the commissioner had at first wanted what the Catholics asked, that the reading already begun be finished. Later, however, the Donatists wrung from him permission to have what they were offering read, and the other documents were postponed.

Then the Donatists made some preliminary remarks. They claimed that Mensurius, who had been bishop of the church of Carthage before Caecilian, had handed over the holy scriptures to the persecutors in time of persecution. To prove this they read his letter to Secundus of Tigisis, who then held the primacy among the bishops of Numidia. In this letter Mensurius seemed to be confessing his crime, as it were. Yet he had not written that he had handed over the holy books. Rather, he wrote that he had removed them and kept them safe so that the persecutors would not find them. In the basilica of the Novae [?] he had left whatever rejected writings of heretics there were, and when the persecutors found these and took them away, nothing more was demanded of him. Afterward, however, certain members of the town council of Carthage suggested to the proconsul that the men sent to take away and burn the Christians' scriptures had been tricked. They had found only some writings or other that had nothing to do with the scriptures, while the scriptures themselves were being kept in the bishop's house, from which they ought to be brought out and burned. But the proconsul refused to go along with them in this. The same letter also related that Mensurius disapproved of those who offered themselves to the persecutors without having been arrested. Though no one had asked them, they declared of their own accord that they had scriptures which they would not hand over, and he had forbidden Christians to honor them. In the same letter certain people were also charged with being criminals and debtors to the treasury. They took persecution as an occasion either to be rid of a life burdened with many debts, or to purge and, as it were, wash away their crimes, as they thought, or at any rate to acquire money and enjoy luxuries in prison from the attentions of Christians.
