Still, the Donatists brought no charge against Mensurius except the handing over of the books. They said that he lied in saying that those were not the holy books, and that he wanted to cover up his sin, though they also condemned the deception itself. They also read the reply of Secundus of Tigisis to Mensurius, written in a peaceable spirit. In it he too related what the persecutors had done in Numidia, and who had been arrested, refused to hand over the holy scriptures, suffered many evils, and been tortured with the most severe punishments and killed. He commended them as worthy of honor for the merit of their martyrdom. He praised them for not handing over the holy scriptures, following the example of the woman in Jericho who refused to hand over to the pursuers the two spies, in whom the two testaments, the Old and the New, were prefigured. If that example is to be understood in this figurative sense, it actually helped Mensurius. In his letter Mensurius blamed those who did not hand over the holy scriptures but nevertheless admitted that they had them, and that woman did not do this: she did not confess that the spies being sought were with her, but denied it. Secundus also wrote that the curator and the council had sent a centurion and a beneficiarius to him to demand the divine books for burning. He answered them: "I am a Christian and a bishop, not a traditor." And when they wanted to take some castoffs from him, or anything at all, he did not give them even this, following the example of Eleazar the Maccabee, who would not even pretend to eat pork, lest he set others an example of transgression. The Catholics listened patiently until these letters of Mensurius and Secundus had been read through to the end, though they declared that these were private letters and had nothing to do with the case of the church.

So the commissioner urged the Donatists to return their patience in kind, and ordered that the documents offered by the Catholics, already partly read, be read through. At this the Donatists demanded that what they were offering about the case of Caecilian also be read first. The Catholics allowed this too without any difficulty, pointing out how patiently they were permitting it, so that the others might repay them in kind, and the commissioner ordered what was offered to be read. The Donatists then read out a council of about seventy bishops held at Carthage against Caecilian. There they condemned him in his absence because he refused to come to them, being, as they claimed, ordained by traditors, and because, when he was a deacon, he was said to have prevented food from being brought to martyrs held in prison. Certain colleagues of Caecilian were also named who were alleged to be traditors on the basis of public records, though these records were not read. Among these Felix of Abthugni in particular was accused with special bitterness, so that he was called the source of all evils. Then the sentences were pronounced one by one, first by Secundus of Tigisis, who was their leader, and then by the rest. In them they declared that they did not hold communion with Caecilian and his colleagues. When this council had been read, the Catholics replied that the letters exchanged between Mensurius and Secundus showed clearly enough that the two were at peace, and that afterward no charge concerning what Mensurius had done was either brought or judged. As for the council against Caecilian which the Donatists had read, it did indeed lack a consul and a date. But the Catholics said they were raising no charge on that account, since this could be due to negligence rather than fraud.

But the Catholics offered another council, held under the same Secundus of Tigisis in the city of Cirta. When its consul and date were read, the Donatists said that decrees of that kind usually have neither consul nor date. Here the Catholics replied that perhaps this was the custom of those who did not want their councils to be convicted of some falsehood, but that the councils of the Catholics had always had consuls and dates. Then the reading of the council the Catholics had brought began. In it Secundus questioned one by one certain men whom he had heard to be guilty of handing over, and when they confessed, he removed them from the assembly. It was read in such a way that, whenever the confession of one of these traditors had been read from the Council of Cirta, that same man's name was also read from the Council of Carthage, where he condemned others as traditors in Caecilian's case. Then they came to the charge brought against Secundus of Tigisis himself by Purpurius of Limata. Secundus had charged Purpurius with killing his sister's sons in the prison at Milevis. Purpurius in turn charged him with handing over, saying that he had been detained by the curator and the council to give up the scriptures, and could not have been released unless he had handed over something. Now Secundus himself almost confessed what Purpurius charged him with, that he had been detained by the curator and the council to give up the scriptures, in the letter he wrote in reply to Mensurius. There he says that a centurion and a beneficiarius had been sent to him by the curator and the council, and that the scriptures, or any castoffs, were demanded of him, though he says he did not hand them over. But he himself mentions there so many martyrs who were tortured and killed when they refused to hand them over. How, then, could he himself be detained, found out, refuse to hand over anything, and yet suffer nothing and be released? He explained this neither in writing to Mensurius nor in answering Purpurius. For he did not tell the centurion and the beneficiarius that he did not have the scriptures; he answered that he would not hand them over at all. Once they had heard this, how they could let him go and report back without bringing ruin on themselves is not apparent. This is especially so because Secundus himself said that not just any lowly people, but even heads of households, had been put to death in the cruelest ways when they gave the persecutors this same answer. But the Catholics charged Secundus with no crime in this matter. They only wanted the charge Purpurius brought against him to be read, along with the fact that because of it, leaving all those things to God, he made peace with the traditors so that a schism would not arise. In this way it would be clear what sort of men had pronounced sentence against Caecilian in his absence.

When this had been read, the Catholics asked that the postponed documents also be read. They asserted that these could show what had been done about Caecilian and what was to be thought of the Council of Carthage, in which, as had been read, Caecilian was condemned in his absence by many bishops. The Donatists, on the other hand, pressed the Catholics to admit that this council was genuine. Their argument was that the Catholics had read the reports of the proconsul Anullinus, which showed that documents with charges against Caecilian had been sent to the emperor Constantine, and by doing so they had certainly confirmed that the forebears of the Donatists had accused Caecilian before the emperor. The Catholics answered that the Council of Carthage did not prejudge Caecilian in his absence, just as the council of those who condemned Primian in the affair of Maximian did not prejudge Primian in his absence. For the party of Donatus held to what was done afterward on Primian's behalf rather than to the authority of the council by which he had earlier been condemned. So in Caecilian's case too, they said, attention must be paid to what was done afterward. Here the Donatists, hemmed in by the case of Maximian, said that one case does not prejudge another, nor one person another. Yet all Catholics are accustomed to have this maxim on their lips whenever the Donatists, holding the crimes of some against others, defended their separation and accused the Christian world on account of some crimes or other committed by Africans. Indeed, in this very conference the Catholics had worked throughout to keep the case of the church distinct from the case of Caecilian, asserting that the wicked mixed into the church do not harm the good or stain them with their sins. Their whole aim had been precisely this: that one case should not prejudge another, nor one person another. And now, while something else was being discussed, their opponents confirmed it in the plainest words. But when the commissioner asked what the Catholics answered about the Council of Carthage, they replied again that the parallel with Primian's case was not to be despised, since the Lord Christ too led the Jews to the truth by convicting them through their own deeds.

Then the Donatists argued at length that Caecilian's condemnation was confirmed by the authority of that Council of Carthage. First, he had refused to come to so many bishops, as if Primian too, recognizing their faction for what it was, had not with a similar will refused to come to those who condemned him. Second, Caecilian had not waited to be ordained as primate by a primate. Yet the custom of the Catholic Church is different: the bishop of the church of Carthage is ordained not by the bishops of Numidia but by bishops nearer at hand. In the same way no metropolitan bishop ordains the bishop of the Roman church either, but the bishop of Ostia, which is close by. In saying this about their own custom, instituted who knows when, they were trying to prejudge the Catholic Church. If that custom had been ancient, they would have charged Caecilian with this very thing when they condemned him in his absence. They also said that Optatus had written that Caecilian said: "If those who ordained me are traditors, let them come and ordain me." If this was in fact said, it could have been said to mock those to whom he is reported to have sent this message, since he was certain that the men who ordained him were not traditors. For he does not say, "since they are traditors," but "if they are traditors," leaving their innocence to be proven where it could properly be proven.

To these points, and to anything else they said in their long pleading, the Catholics replied briefly. They said that the Council of Carthage was not enough to settle Caecilian's case even in the judgment of the very men who had sent the case to the emperor as accusers. By doing so they had shown that what mattered more was that the affair had gone all the way to the emperor's sentence, since they themselves had thought fit to send the same case to him. The Catholics kept pressing for this: that every shady hiding place of delay be cut away, and that the documents be read instead which, once read, had ended the case long ago, so that Caecilian's proven innocence would appear clearer than daylight. The Donatists were entirely unwilling to have these read and kept blocking it by putting forward anything else at all. When the judge asked whether the Council of Carthage had been held first and Caecilian's case sent to the emperor afterwards, the Catholics said that, since that council bore no consul and no date, they would answer both possibilities. If the case had been sent to the emperor first, one ought to look at the outcome that concluded it. If it was sent afterwards, then one should still look not to the bishops' judgment but to the judgment of the one to whom they themselves had thought it should be sent after giving their own. The Donatists then brought in a great deal about the consul and the date, explaining why none was read in their forebears' council, so that they would not be convicted of forgery on that score. They asserted that it was church custom not to write dates and consuls into the decrees of bishops, and they wanted even the council of Cyprian read to prove it, since they were seeking nothing but delay. The Catholics had not rested their case on this point, since they had answered both possibilities, whether that council the Donatists had held against Caecilian at Carthage came earlier or later. So, at the Catholics' urging, the judge ordered that the documents that had been put off should be read instead.

Then the Donatists brought up another question, one full of delays, but one in which they really wanted to work for their own side, if they could show what they wished. They wanted to show that the Council of Cirta was a forgery. At that council the confessions of traditors had been read, who pardoned one another to avoid a schism, and these same men were read to have been among those who pronounced sentence against Caecilian in his absence. In trying to prove it forged they said many things, but they themselves judged the rest to be trivial and laid great stress on two points, dwelling on them at length. The first was that the Council of Cirta bore a date and a consul, contrary to church custom. The second was that a council could not have been assembled in a time of persecution. So the Donatists demanded that the Catholics either produce other ancient councils of bishops in which consuls and dates were also written, or read out something of the kind from the holy Scriptures themselves. The Catholics saw that astonishing, endless delays were being put in the way over an utterly empty matter. Who would have believed that the Donatists would allege forgery on this ground, when a record of the date was read at the head of the document for greater exactness, in case an inquiry into the truth should someday require it? Who would have believed they would raise this objection, so that anyone would have prepared ancient councils to demonstrate this custom? Or who would go off at that moment and turn over the old church archives? Seeing this, the Catholics both pointed out the date and consul in the council of Miltiades and recalled from the holy Scriptures themselves that the prophets had set at the head of their writings indications of the most ancient times: in what year of which king, in what month of the year, on what day of the month the word of the Lord had come upon them. The judge, however, thought that this objection about date and consul should be dismissed and set aside, and he ordered the rest of the proceedings held before Miltiades to be read, and they were read. They made it plain that Caecilian had been acquitted and cleared by the sentences of all the bishops who sat at that time, and of Miltiades himself. Donatus, on the other hand, had been condemned after being convicted in person at the first hearing. This was that Donatus of Casae Nigrae, who was established to have been present at the time.

When this had been read, the Donatists were asked what answer they had to the Council of Cirta. They went back to trying to show it was a forgery, saying that a council could not have been assembled in a time of persecution. The judge did not dismiss this. He thought it a strong point and asked the Catholics for a reply, and in the meantime he asked how it was proved that it had been a time of persecution. Then the Donatists produced the acts of martyrs who had been tried and had suffered for their confession. The judge also ordered his staff to compute and report the interval, taking into account both sets of consuls and dates, the ones read from the Council of Cirta and the ones read from the acts of the martyrs. The Catholics had said that after the passion of those martyrs, which proved the time of persecution, nearly a year had passed before the consul and date of the Council of Cirta. The staff's computation, however, indicated that a month had intervened. So the Catholics wanted what they had said struck from the record, so that the proceedings would keep only the staff's answer, because they believed it was more accurate. But the Donatists refused to have the Catholics' statement struck from the record, and the Catholics did not argue the point, so that the Donatists' captious spirit would be plain. In fact what the Catholics had said was more accurate, and the staff had made a mistake in its computation and reported wrongly. The proceedings showed this later, once they were written up and examined more carefully, as anyone can verify who cares to read them and does not mind counting. The acts of the martyrs, which showed the time of persecution, were drawn up in the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth, on the day before the Ides of February. The episcopal proceedings with the decree of Cirta were dated after their consulship, on the third day before the Nones of March. So thirteen months are found to lie between them, certainly more than the eleven the Catholics had given earlier in their less careful reckoning. The staff went wrong and answered that one month intervened because they took it to be the same consulship and did not notice the words 'after the consulship', when another year was already under way. As a result, the Catholics were forced to proceed as though the staff's answer were correct and to show that in a time of persecution those eleven or twelve bishops could have met in a private house. The Donatists pressed them to show this from other councils, if they could find any councils of bishops held at some time of persecution. The Catholics could not search for these then and there or go through old documents in the church archives. So they replied that it was much easier for twelve men to gather in a house at a time when even congregations of the people regularly met, though persecution was raging. This was shown by the very acts of those martyrs, who confessed during their passions that they had held the assembly and celebrated the Lord's rite. The Catholics had said this even before the staff computed and answered. The Catholics also said that those episcopal proceedings of Cirta, which the diligence of their forebears had managed to preserve and bring to light down to the present day, should be treated the same way as those letters of Mensurius and Secundus that the Donatists had read. The Council of Carthage, where seventy bishops condemned Caecilian in his absence, is also mentioned in the council held by Miltiades, where Caecilian was acquitted. Those letters of Mensurius and Secundus, on the other hand, were said to be mentioned nowhere else, so no other testimony vouched for their genuineness. Even so, the Catholics did not say on that account that they were forged. The Catholics also said that the Donatists should prove, if they could, that in a time of persecution bishops had written to one another in the way they claimed Mensurius and Secundus had written. The Catholics did not say this in order to show that those letters were forged, since whether genuine or forged they did the case no harm. They said it so that the Donatists would see what an empty evasion it was to force the Catholics to produce other councils assembled in a time of persecution. Suppose someone said to them with the same obstinacy: 'You too must produce other letters written and sent like this in a time of persecution. If such letters had somehow been intercepted, and the hidden books could then have been demanded, the town council, the curator, the centurion and the beneficiarius would all have been put in danger of their lives, since the letter exposed them as having let Secundus go unpunished when he refused to hand the books over.' They would have had no way of finding, then and there, other letters sent in the same way by bishops to bishops in a time of persecution across such distant lands.

So a long struggle arose from this. The Donatists repeated again and again that a council could not have been gathered to ordain a bishop in a time of persecution, because the world was in apostasy and there was no one for whom a bishop could be ordained, and so on. The Catholics replied that bishops so few that it should not even be called a council could easily gather when congregations were gathering, as the acts of the martyrs testified. They added that there were without doubt people for whom bishops could be ordained, namely those very congregations which, according to the acts of the martyrs, regularly gathered at that time. These things were said and answered constantly in many different ways. It was also established that a private house had been provided for gathering Christians in a time of persecution, as was read in certain acts of martyrs, since the Donatists had said it was impossible that anyone at that time would offer his house. It was further pointed out that it was so far from incredible that those few bishops met in a private house in a time of persecution that, even while persecution raged, martyrs are shown to have been baptized in prison, and the sacraments to have been celebrated there by Christians in the very place where Christians were held locked up because of those same sacraments. Amid all this, the judge, who had often interjected that the bishops could have held that meeting when the congregations were also proved to have gathered, at long last compelled the Donatists to say whatever they had against the council and judgment of Miltiades. That judgment was read to have cleared and acquitted Caecilian, and the case rested on it rather than on the Council of Cirta.

Then the Donatists began to accuse Miltiades himself of the crime of handing over the Scriptures. They said their forebears had avoided his judgment because he had been a traditor, as if they had not appeared at his tribunal and answered that they had nothing to say against Caecilian. The judge then became intent on whether any judgment, public or ecclesiastical, would be produced on a charge of handing over against Miltiades, and the Catholics themselves were waiting for it to be proved and demanding that it should be. The Donatists then read some very lengthy proceedings held before a prefect, in which it was not clear what kind of prefect he was, and the place where these things were done was not read out. Those proceedings, in a very long reading, rang with the names of many people handing over many church possessions, but the name of Miltiades was not heard at all. When the reading was finished, the judge was surprised that one thing had been promised and another read. Still begging his patience, they read other proceedings, in which it was read that Miltiades had sent deacons to the prefect of the city with letters from the emperor Maxentius and from the praetorian prefect. The deacons were to recover the property that had been taken away in the time of persecution and that the emperor had ordered returned to the Christians. These proceedings too showed no crime of Miltiades, either to the judge or to the Catholic advocates. So the Donatists said that the deacon Strato, whom Miltiades had sent with others to recover the church properties, had been read as a traditor in the earlier proceedings. On that basis they wanted to smear Miltiades too with the crime of handing over, because he employed that deacon without deposing him. In their pleading, however, they said that Miltiades was the third bishop after the one who held office when that handing over took place. Here the judge asked whether those proceedings about the handing over at least stated expressly that Strato was a deacon. What was read was that he was called a 'promoter of a most vain superstition', the name given not only to him but to the others who handed things over. But the Donatists replied that the pagan persecutors called both deacons and presbyters by that name as an insult to the religion.

The Catholics replied that it is nothing strange, and indeed very common in human affairs, for not just two but many people to be called by the same name. It could well be, then, that the traditor Strato was a presbyter and this other Strato a deacon, since the Donatists had said that pagans called both deacons and presbyters promoters of a most vain superstition. In fact pagans could have called all clerics by that insulting name, which made it even less certain what rank that traditor cleric held. And even if he could be shown to have been a deacon, that too would be neither incredible nor strange, since not long ago there had been two deacons named Peter in the very city of Rome. The Catholics added a further point. Suppose it were proved, which it was not at all, that the same deacon Strato whom Miltiades later sent with other deacons to recover the church properties had handed the Scriptures over. Even then Miltiades would not automatically be stained by that crime. The persecution may have kept him far away, so that he knew nothing of it at all and thought the man innocent, since no one had brought an accusation to show him guilty. Against this the Donatists went on shouting the same things over and over for a very long time, to no purpose.

After the conference, in fact, they also brought a false charge against Miltiades concerning Cassian. This name too is found both among the deacons whom Miltiades sent to the prefect and in the proceedings where the act of handing over was read. Had they said this at the conference, the Catholics could easily have replied that in so large a crowd of Roman clergy it would be no wonder to find two or more Cassians as well as Stratos, since among the twelve apostles we read of two Judases and also of two Jameses. Or were the Donatists perhaps allowed to distinguish Donatus of Casae from Donatus of Carthage, when they feared that their greater founder, Donatus of Carthage, would be thought to have been condemned at Miltiades' tribunal, while the Catholics were not allowed to have several men with the same names in so great a multitude of Roman clergy? What the Donatists had said was false, namely that the persons matched, the places matched and the districts matched. Neither the places nor the districts, nor even the ranks of the persons, were stated in both sets of proceedings. All that was read was a coincidence of names, and human usage never stops repeating names among different persons.

So the judge rejected these utterly uncertain suspicions and ordered that something clear be produced against those proceedings, or at any rate that the judgment of Constantine, which had already been mentioned, be read. Constantine's judgment was read. In it he wrote to Eumalius, vicar of Africa, telling how he had heard Caecilian's case between the parties. With all onlookers removed, he testified, he had found Caecilian innocent and his accusers utterly malicious. He also mentioned the episcopal judgment given for Caecilian in the town of Arles. Very many of the dissenting party had already accepted that judgment, while the rest still held back and kept up their quarrel, and for that reason he was compelled to judge the whole matter himself between the parties. After this imperial letter was read, the judge asked the Donatists what they had to say against it. At that point the Donatists tried to go back to their slanderous charge against Miltiades. When the judge's ruling had driven them off it, they were asked to read whatever they had against the judgment of Miltiades or the imperial sentence. They replied that even the emperor's ears had been swollen with wicked suggestions. The judge answered that he had noted very carefully that the case had been judged between the parties. Then they began demanding that the passage be read to show whether the emperor had judged between the parties. It was read at the judge's order, and when they found nothing to say, they began to make a captious objection about the consul of that imperial letter, because it had been read without a consul. This set off a quarrel. The Donatists said, to stir up ill will, that the episcopal council had been read with a consul while the emperor's letter had none. The Catholics replied that the case did not rest on that. The judge also ruled that it is laid down by the plainest laws that imperial enactments are not called into doubt even if no consuls are read in them. Then the Catholics pressed the Donatists to say openly that what had been read was forged, since the archives could be searched.

Driven back from this, they asked for Optatus to be read, as though about to produce something very strong. They had asked for this before and said it would prove that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor. It had been promised to them but put off. The judge first wanted them to state plainly whether they dared to charge the imperial letter with forgery. This they did not dare at all, yet they still complained, with great show of indignation, that the consul was missing, and they demanded far more insistently that Optatus be read. While this went on for some time, the consul of that imperial letter was found in another copy. When this was reported, the Donatists said, 'Surely it ought not to have had a consul', as if anyone had ever said that it ought not to have one, rather than that, even if the consul were missing, this would not affect the genuineness of the imperial enactment. The judge gave them this answer more than once, and then Optatus was read, the Donatists themselves reading the passage where he says: 'At the same time this same Donatus asked to be allowed to return and go to Carthage. Then Philomenus, his advocate, suggested to the emperor that for the sake of peace Caecilian should be detained at Brescia, and it was done.' In these words of Optatus no condemnation of Caecilian at all could be found, though they had promised to demonstrate one. So the judge ordered the whole page to be read, so that the writer's meaning could be known from the words before and after. The staff read: 'By the sentences of all those mentioned above, Caecilian was declared innocent.' When this was read, the Donatists said they had not asked for it to be read, and they were annoyed with those who could not keep from laughing on hearing what a plain page against themselves they had brought forward. Then they said that in the words they had read Optatus had played down Caecilian's condemnation and had not wanted to state it outright. They were asked to read from elsewhere a clear statement of what they said he had played down. This they could not do at all. They also argued about the name of Donatus, saying that it was Donatus of Casae, not Donatus of Carthage, who had stood against Caecilian at Miltiades' tribunal, a point the Catholics also granted. Finally, after a good many tangles of empty delay, they moved on from this as well.

The judge then pressed them to answer, if they had anything, Constantine's letter, which established that he had heard the case between the parties and judged for Caecilian against them. They asked for their own petition to be read, which they said their forebears had presented to Constantine. In that petition they showed plainly enough how false their claim about Caecilian's condemnation at Brescia had been, for the same petition shows how Constantine had judged against them. In it they say that they will in no way be in communion with 'his bishop, that worthless fellow', and that they are ready to suffer whatever he might choose to do to them. By Constantine's worthless bishop they certainly meant Caecilian to be understood. So how could they call him Constantine's bishop, while declaring in defiance of Constantine that they would not be in communion with him, if they had defeated him before Constantine, so that they knew he had been condemned by the emperor at Brescia?

The Catholics said that the Donatists had read this out against themselves, and the judge himself said the same in an interlocutory remark. The Donatists then added another strong proof of their own falsehood by reading a letter of Constantine himself to Verinus the vicar, in which he tells him to leave them to their free choice and indicates that he has ordered them to return from exile. In this letter Constantine denounces them so strongly that nothing could be more shameful for them than that act of leniency. He would surely not have blamed them like this, but would rather have praised them, if Caecilian had been defeated by them before him, condemned by him and banished to Brescia. So by producing and reading these documents against themselves, they showed very plainly that they had been defeated by Caecilian in the judgment of that emperor, and they clearly proved false their own claim that Caecilian had been condemned. They used to boast that the Catholics were the persecutors and they the persecuted, yet they also wanted to boast, falsely, that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor on their accusations. After these documents had been read, the Catholics said, and briefly reminded the judge of what he himself could see, that they had been read in the Catholics' favour, that is, for Caecilian's innocence and against the Donatists, and the judge had said the same in an interlocutory remark. The Donatists answered: 'Your Authority says nothing about free choice.' They thought that, on the strength of Constantine's letter, this could be granted them by the present judge, and that was why they decided the letter should be read even though it told against them and for Caecilian's cause. When the judge answered that he had received different orders from the present emperor, they turned to something else, which they again produced against themselves, and far more remarkably.

For they read another letter of the same Emperor Constantine, addressed to Probianus the proconsul. This letter had no consular date, but the Catholics did not wish to make anything of this, as though answering one objection with another. Yet here too the Donatists convicted themselves of how slanderously they had raised that objection against the Catholics, since the first sheet, from which Constantine's judgment acquitting Caecilian had been read, had no consuls, though they were soon found on another sheet. This letter to Probianus the proconsul contains the emperor's command that Ingentius be sent to him. It was by Ingentius' confession, in the court of the proconsul Aelianus, that Felix of Abthugni, who had ordained Caecilian, had been acquitted of the charge of handing over the Scriptures. The Donatists said they were reading this imperial command in order to show, as they supposed, that Caecilian's case was still undecided even after the judgment in which Constantine had already written that he had settled everything between the parties. Yet in this very letter to Probianus, which they read to show that the judgment was still pending because the emperor had ordered Ingentius to be sent to him, they read so much against themselves that it is truly astonishing with what eyes they could look at it or with what face they could read it aloud. For in it Constantine said that the proconsul Aelianus had given the matter a proper hearing and that Felix had been shown to be innocent of burning the sacred books, but that those who did not cease petitioning him day after day must be refuted in his presence, so that it might be clear to them that they had sought in vain to stir up hatred against Caecilian and to rise up violently against him. Here, then, through this letter, they showed that not only Caecilian but Felix too had been cleared, and that they themselves had appeared before the emperor as persecutors of innocent men.

Taking this opportunity, the Catholics produced for reading the report on this matter that Aelianus, then proconsul, had sent to Constantine, in which he records that he had heard and concluded Felix's case. They also produced the proconsular proceedings themselves, by which Felix was acquitted and proved innocent of the crime of handing over the Scriptures by the testimony of all the necessary witnesses. When these had been read, the judge asked what could be said against them. Then the Donatists repeated over and over what they had already begun to say: they asked whether Ingentius had been sent to court by the emperor's order, and demanded that the Catholics show what had happened afterward. They tried to find words to refute the proconsular proceedings by which Felix had been acquitted, alleging favouritism on the judge's part, or that the witnesses had been planted, and all the other things that people commonly toss about with suspicious complaints against records that go against them. They also said that Felix had not been rightly acquitted in his absence. To this the Catholics replied that everything that had been read bore most plainly on the acquittal of Caecilian and Felix. If the Donatists thought that, after Ingentius had been sent to court, a judgment had been given in their favour and the earlier judgment changed, the judgment in which Constantine, hearing the parties, had cleared Caecilian and found them guilty of the grossest slander, then they ought to produce it themselves. When the Catholics said this, there was no chance in so short a time to examine the consular dates. But anyone who cares to examine their order in the proceedings themselves will find that Caecilian was acquitted by the Emperor Constantine after Felix's case had been examined and cleared by the proconsul Aelianus. He will also find that some years later Constantine wrote the letter to Verinus the vicar which the Donatists themselves read, claiming that it granted them free choice from that emperor, and that in this letter he shows them to be utterly wicked and enemies of Christian peace. He would surely not have done that if he had given any judgment in their favour against Caecilian when Ingentius was sent to court. The judge therefore ruled that proceedings confirmed by such great antiquity could not be set aside unless other, later proceedings to the contrary were read. The Catholics also said that Felix's acquittal in his absence did more to establish his innocence, because if he had been present a suspicion of favouritism would more likely have arisen.

The judge then began to press the Donatists to produce at once any later proceedings they had against the acquittal of Caecilian or of Felix. At this they tried once again to go back, as it were, to the beginning and to rehearse the points they had already made so many times, which had been dealt with as the Catholics answered every one of them again and again. The judge interrupted, urging them to be ashamed by now of repeating things that had been dealt with and settled, and pressed them repeatedly to produce anything they had to read against such clear acquittals of Caecilian and Felix. They produced nothing at all against these, but would not stop repeating the same things and demanding a judgment on what they had said, while the judge insisted instead that they read anything they had that could be read against the imperial and proconsular judgments, so that he could pronounce on everything, since the laws forbid giving a half-complete sentence. The Catholics also urged that, since everything had been made clear to the judge and the Donatists could find no answer but kept repeating the same things, the case should at last be brought to an end. Finally the judge said: 'If there is nothing you can read against this, please withdraw, so that a full sentence can be written on everything.' Both sides withdrew and he wrote his sentence. When the parties were brought back in, he read it out. In it he covered everything he could remember from the long three days' proceedings. Some things he recorded out of the order in which they had happened, but he set everything down truthfully, declaring that the Donatists had been refuted by the Catholics through the clear evidence of all the documents.
A Summary of the Conference with the Donatists, in Three Books.

After our conference with the Donatists had taken place, I gave a brief account of what was done and set it down in writing according to the three days on which we met with them. I judged this a useful work, because anyone who consults it can either learn without effort what took place or, by checking the numbers I have noted beside each item, read whatever passage they wish at its place in the proceedings themselves, since those proceedings weary the reader with their excessive length. The title of this work is: A Summary of the Conference.
